name: Laser lipolysis (SmartLipo)

card.summary: Laser-assisted fat removal that heats fat through a small cannula, with early studies reporting fat reduction and some skin tightening.
card.note: A minimally invasive surgical procedure; published work is mostly small series and tissue studies.

quick.overview:
Laser lipolysis, best known by the SmartLipo brand, is a minimally invasive procedure in which a laser fiber is passed through a small incision to liquefy or heat fat, often followed by suction. It is discussed in looksmaxxing spaces for the jawline and neck.

The early literature, much of it practitioner-written, reports fat reduction and skin tightening. Most published studies are small, histology or modeling studies, or retrospective series.
quick.mechanism: Laser energy at wavelengths such as 1064, 1320 or 1444 nm is absorbed by fat tissue, disrupting fat cells and heating the surrounding tissue. Authors claim the heating also stimulates collagen and skin contraction.
quick.risks: It is a surgical procedure with risks shared with liposuction, such as bleeding, infection, numbness and contour irregularities. Heating of tissue is a specific consideration, and thermal studies have examined temperature rise in treated tissue.

lead: Laser lipolysis, also called laser-assisted liposuction or by the SmartLipo brand, uses laser energy delivered through a thin fiber under the skin to disrupt fat cells, sometimes followed by suction removal. It is promoted for small areas, including the neck and jawline, and for tightening skin [1][7].

Early reports described a less traumatic technique than conventional liposuction with reduced bleeding and skin retraction [1]. Subsequent work includes a 30-subject Nd:YAG study [2], histologic and thermal studies [3][4], and a retrospective analysis of 534 procedures with a diode laser [8]. General liposuction carries recognized risks, which a Wikipedia overview summarizes [11].

paras: A thin laser fiber is introduced through a small incision into subcutaneous fat. The laser interacts with fat tissue, and the loosened fat may then be suctioned. Authors describe a less traumatic technique than conventional liposuction [1].

Histologic work on a pulsed Nd:YAG device (SmartLipo) examined its effects on excised human fat tissue [4]. Other studies compared wavelengths of 1064, 1320 and 2100 nm ex vivo [9], and examined tissue temperature rise during 1064/1320 nm treatment [3]. A mathematical modeling paper described laser lipolysis heat effects [6], and a study compared a 1,444 nm laser with a 1,064 nm laser, reporting a superior lipolytic effect for the former [10].

An early report described skin retraction in flaccid areas [1]. A 2006 study of 30 subjects with small fat areas used a 1,064 nm Nd:YAG laser, with MRI in some participants at baseline and 3 months [2]. A 2009 retrospective analysis of 534 procedures with a 980-nm diode laser has been published [8], and a 2016 paper described a combination approach to neck rejuvenation including laser lipolysis [7].

Liposuction in general has reported complications including infection, bleeding, numbness, seroma and contour irregularities, with rare serious events [11]. Thermal studies of laser lipolysis examine how much tissue heating occurs at different wavelengths and techniques [3].

Published human work is largely small prospective studies and retrospective series [1][2][8]. Several small trials of related devices are registered: a 1440 nm laser for the mandible and submandibular area (n=12, completed) [13], an LED device for non-invasive lipolysis (n=10, terminated) [12], a 1060 nm diode laser with other energy for non-invasive fat reduction (n=39, completed) [15], laser therapy with aerobic exercise (n=36, terminated) [14], and a 1064 nm diode laser/RF study (withdrawn) [16]. Results are not given in the available records.
